extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists (students and researchers) writing exposition and papers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for clear, correct, and effective mathematical/technical exposition (sentence-level style, word choice, punctuation, organization, and proof presentation) aimed at CS/math students and researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability grade (grade-level indices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style routines produce readability grades using a linear formula: grade = α(words/sentence) + β(syllables/word) + γ, where α, β, γ are fit by regression against texts assigned subjective grade levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to minimise the grade level to make prose more readable, but do not overdo it so that the purpose or subtlety is lost. Readability tools also report sentence length stats, parts-of-speech percentages, and passive-voice counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average sentence length and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs report average sentence length and the percentage of sentences much shorter or longer than the average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer shorter sentences when clarity is at risk; cut long sentences into two where appropriate. Avoid many long, complex sentences that separate subject and verb. Use sentence-length statistics to find problem areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive voice (avoidance and detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence is considered 'passive' if a passive verb appears anywhere in it (even in a subclause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active constructions to improve clarity and directness. Where passive is standard or inoffensive, it may be acceptable; rewrite examples: 'Each of the ∆z’s are then multiplied by this factor' → 'Multiply each ∆z by this factor.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction flags (questionable words/phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: A diction tool flags a set of ~450 words/phrases deemed 'questionable' (examples: 'gratuitous', 'number of', 'due to', 'very', 'literally', 'in fact', 'which').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alternatives suggested (e.g. avoid 'number of', prefer more direct phrasing). Accept about half of automated suggestions—machines help but should not override authorial judgment. Note domain exceptions (e.g. mathematical use of 'due to' to credit a theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weak intensifiers like 'very'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'very' is singled out as a suspect intensifier.
